_readme: Hydration-step product pack for the K-beauty library — toners, essences, emulsions, mists, sheet masks and sleeping masks. Consumed by build-kbeauty-pages.cjs via the kbeauty-products-*.json glob. Same contract as the rest of the library: cosmetic structure-function wording, hedged claims, no invented statistics or INCI lists, no medical advice. Every entry names a real caveat. Formulas are revised often — copy describes products from public information, never from a claimed formula percentage.

products.name: Heartleaf 77% Soothing Toner
products.whatItIs: A watery toner built on heartleaf — 어성초 (eoseongcho), Houttuynia cordata — which forms the bulk of the water phase rather than sitting near the bottom of the list as a token extract. There are no acids, no added fragrance and no colourant. What you get is a thin, fast-absorbing layer of 진정 (jinjeong, calming) hydration with panthenol alongside. It became Anua's global bestseller largely on that simplicity.
products.whoItSuits: Best for reactive, flushed or lightly congested skin that wants a hydration step which does not also introduce an active. Oily and combination skin will like how little it leaves behind. Very dry skin will find it thin — treat it as the first of several layers, not the whole job. It is not a spot treatment, and people expecting it to clear breakouts are usually disappointed.
products.howToUse: First hydration step after cleansing, morning and night. Two or three passes with damp hands rather than a soaked cotton pad — the 7-skin idea works well here because the texture is so light. Follow with an essence or serum, then seal with moisturiser. Nothing in it conflicts with retinol, acids or vitamin C.
products.watchOut: The 77% figure describes how much heartleaf water is in the formula, not how strong it is — a high proportion of a mild extract is still mild. Reviews crediting it with clearing acne are overstating things; evidence for topical Houttuynia is thin and mostly points at soothing. Persistent breakouts are a conversation for a clinician, not a toner.

products.name: 1025 Dokdo Toner
products.whatItIs: Round Lab's flagship, named for the coordinates of the Dokdo islets whose deep-sea mineral water forms its base. The formula is deliberately unremarkable: mineral water, humectants, panthenol, a little betaine, no fragrance and no essential oils. It belongs to the category of toners designed to be boring on purpose — a plain water-and-humectant layer you can use twice a day for years without your skin objecting.
products.whoItSuits: A safe default for sensitive, barrier-stressed or newly reactive skin, and a sensible first Korean toner for anyone who has been burnt by fragranced products. Dry skin will need something richer layered over it. If you want visible brightening or exfoliation from a toner this is the wrong bottle — it does hydration and nothing else, by design.
products.howToUse: Straight after cleansing, AM and PM, patted in with hands. Two thin layers on damp skin do more than one heavy one. Fine underneath any active, and useful as a buffer on nights you use retinol or an exfoliant. A cotton pad works but wastes a good deal of product.
products.watchOut: The deep-sea mineral water story is doing more work than the ingredient does — mineral content at these levels is not a demonstrated skincare benefit. Judge it as a well-made, fragrance-free humectant toner, which it is, rather than as something special from Ulleungdo. A few people find the slight slip takes a moment to settle under sunscreen.

products.name: Hyaluronic Acid Toner
products.whatItIs: A hydration-only toner built on hyaluronic acid at several molecular weights rather than one, which is why it feels slightly more substantial than a plain water toner without turning tacky. Isntree keeps the rest short: humectants, a soothing extract or two, no added fragrance in the current version. It is the closest thing Korean drugstore skincare has to a plain glass of water for your face.
products.whoItSuits: Dehydrated skin of any type — including oily skin that is short of water rather than oil. It layers well under heavier creams for dry skin and works alone under sunscreen for oily skin. Sensitive skin generally tolerates it. If your problem is genuinely low oil rather than low water, a toner will not solve it; you need an occlusive step.
products.howToUse: Apply to skin still damp from cleansing, AM and PM, then follow within a minute or two with something that seals it in. Humectants draw water from wherever they can find it, so a hyaluronic layer left bare in dry air can end up feeling tighter rather than softer. Two layers maximum for most people.
products.watchOut: Isntree has reformulated this line more than once, so the bottle you buy may not match a review from two years ago — read the current list. In dry indoor winter air, hyaluronic acid alone can feel counterproductive unless it is sealed. And nothing here addresses redness, texture or tone, whatever the glass-skin marketing implies.

products.name: Green Tea Fresh Toner
products.whatItIs: The oily-skin counterpart to Isntree's hyaluronic toner: a thin, fast-drying water layer based on green tea with soothing humectants behind it. There are no acids, which is unusual for a toner aimed at oily skin — the idea is hydration and calm rather than decongestion, on the reasonable premise that stripping oily skin tends to make it oilier.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and combination skin, particularly in summer or a humid climate, and breakout-prone skin already using an exfoliant elsewhere that does not want a second one. Dry or mature skin will find it too slight. Anyone hoping a green tea toner will hold sebum in check across a whole day should temper expectations considerably.
products.howToUse: After cleansing, morning and night, two thin layers on damp skin. It disappears quickly, which makes it an easy AM step under sunscreen. Follow with a light gel moisturiser rather than skipping the seal — oily skin still needs one, and skipping it is a common reason oily routines stall.
products.watchOut: Green tea polyphenols are genuinely antioxidant in a lab setting, but how much survives in a water toner and how long it stays on skin make any meaningful effect hard to claim. Treat this as a light hydrator that happens to smell faintly of tea. It will not shrink pores — nothing topical does.

products.name: Supple Preparation Facial Toner
products.whatItIs: One of the toners that introduced Western buyers to the idea that a Korean toner hydrates rather than strips. It is a slightly viscous, mildly acidic layer of humectants with centella and other plant extracts, positioned as preparation for whatever follows. Klairs also sells an unscented version, which matters more than usual here, because the original is perfumed with essential oils.
products.whoItSuits: Dry and normal skin that wants a comforting, slightly cushioned first layer. Sensitive skin should go straight to the unscented version rather than testing the original. Oily skin sometimes finds the scented one a touch heavy under sunscreen. It is a general hydrator, not a treatment — it will not move the needle on pigmentation or breakouts.
products.howToUse: After cleansing, AM and PM, patted into damp skin. Two layers if your skin is thirsty. It sits comfortably under acids or retinol as a buffer layer. Give it half a minute to absorb before the next step, or it can pill underneath thicker creams and silicone-containing sunscreens.
products.watchOut: The original formula contains lavender and other essential oils. They smell pleasant and are a well-documented trigger for reactive and eczema-prone skin — if you flush or itch easily, buy the unscented version. The two are otherwise close enough in performance that there is little reason to choose the scented one on merit.

products.name: Essence Toner
products.whatItIs: A very short ingredient list led by Coptis japonica root extract, with a texture closer to a thin essence than a watery toner — slightly slippery, noticeably more substantial than most first steps. Pyunkang Yul built the brand on this minimalism: few ingredients, no added fragrance, no colourant. It is the toner people tend to reach for when everything else has started to sting.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, tight, over-exfoliated or generally fed-up skin, and anyone deliberately assembling a short routine. Mature skin usually appreciates the extra slip. Oily and acne-prone skin sometimes find it too rich for a first step in summer. If you want actives from your toner, look elsewhere — the whole point is that there are almost none.
products.howToUse: One or two layers after cleansing, AM and PM, pressed in rather than swept. Because it is thicker than a typical toner you generally need less of it. On a stripped-back routine it can go straight under a cream with nothing in between. Safe alongside any active you already use.
products.watchOut: That silky finish comes from the humectant base, and some people read it as residue that never quite absorbs — under sunscreen or makeup it can feel like an extra layer. The minimalism is real, but a short ingredient list is not automatically gentler; it only means there are fewer things present to react to.

products.name: SoonJung pH 5.5 Relief Toner
products.whatItIs: The toner from ETUDE's SoonJung range — 순정 (sunjeong, roughly 'pure and gentle') — formulated around panthenol and madecassoside at a mildly acidic pH close to skin's own. It is fragrance-free, colourant-free and built to the minimum-irritant brief Korean brands apply to sensitive-skin lines. Cheap, widely stocked, and one of the least eventful things you can put on your face.
products.whoItSuits: Reactive, flushed or barrier-compromised skin, and anyone recovering from over-exfoliation. It is also a sound beginner toner for teenage skin that is oily but easily irritated. Very dry skin will find it thin on its own. There is nothing in it for pigmentation, lines or pores, and it makes no pretence otherwise.
products.howToUse: First step after cleansing, twice a day. Pat in with hands on damp skin and layer twice if needed. Useful on retinol or acid nights as a calming buffer applied before and after the active. Follow with a cream, particularly if your skin runs dry or the weather has turned.
products.watchOut: 'Relief' is doing a lot of work in that name. It calms the look of irritation and adds water; it does not fix an underlying condition. Redness, stinging or flaking that persists for weeks is a reason to see a dermatologist rather than buy another gentle toner. Gentleness also has a ceiling — a thin toner rarely does the heavy lifting on a damaged barrier.

products.name: Cream Skin Refiner
products.whatItIs: Laneige's attempt to collapse two steps into one: a moisturiser broken down into a milky, pourable liquid so it can be applied like a toner. White leaf tea water forms the base and there is a ceramide element in the emulsion. It feels like thin milk, sinks in quickly, and leaves a soft finish rather than a film you can feel sitting there.
products.whoItSuits: Dry and normal skin that finds a full cream heavy, and anyone who wants a shorter routine without giving up comfort. It suits mature skin well. Oily skin can use it as a summer moisturiser in its own right. Very dry skin in winter will still want a proper cream over the top — the two-in-one idea only stretches so far.
products.howToUse: Use it as your toner step, AM and PM: a coin-sized pour pressed in with the hands, layered two or three times if your skin is dry. On humid days it can stand in for a light moisturiser altogether. Give it a moment to settle before sunscreen so nothing pills.
products.watchOut: It is fragranced, and noticeably so — a genuine problem if you react to perfume. The 'toner and moisturiser in one' positioning is marketing more than formulation: this is a light emulsion, and light emulsions have existed for decades. At the price, what you are mainly buying over a drugstore lotion is texture and finish.

products.name: Madagascar Centella Toning Toner
products.whatItIs: A watery toner whose base is Centella asiatica extract sourced from Madagascar, which is the entire premise of the brand. It is thin, mildly acidic and unfragranced in the current formula. 'Toning' here carries the Korean sense of the word — rebalancing after cleansing — rather than exfoliating or brightening, which is a reliable source of confusion for buyers outside Korea.
products.whoItSuits: Skin that flushes easily, or breakout-prone skin that cannot tolerate the acids usually aimed at it. Oily and combination skin will like the weightlessness. Dry skin needs something layered over it before long. It is a maintenance product: useful as a daily calm-and-hydrate step, unremarkable if you are shopping for visible change.
products.howToUse: After cleansing, morning and night, two light layers on damp skin, then continue with your essence or serum. It works as a buffer either side of an exfoliant. If you also use the brand's centella ampoule, the toner goes first — the thinnest-to-thickest rule holds throughout.
products.watchOut: Centella is one of the better-evidenced soothing botanicals, but a diluted extract in a leave-on water layer is a long way from the concentrations used in research. Expect comfort, not correction. 'Toning' does not mean brightening here, and buyers who read it that way consistently come away underwhelmed.

products.name: Rice Toner
products.whatItIs: A milky, slightly viscous toner built on rice extract with niacinamide alongside. I'm From's approach is single-origin ingredients at a high proportion, with the growing region named on the box, and this is the product that carried the brand abroad. It reads more like a thin essence than a toner and leaves skin looking soft and faintly luminous straight after application.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, dull or textured skin that wants a comfortable hydration step with some glow to it. Mature skin does well with it. Oily skin sometimes finds it too much for a first layer in summer. If your main concern is stubborn pigmentation, the niacinamide here is a supporting player rather than the main event — a dedicated serum will do more.
products.howToUse: After cleansing, AM and PM. Pour into the palm and press in; cotton pads waste it. One layer is usually enough given the texture, two on very dry days. Follow with a serum and cream. It pairs happily with vitamin C in the morning and with retinol at night.
products.watchOut: The glow is hydration plus light reflection, and it fades as the layer dries down — no rice extract is remodelling your skin tone overnight. It carries a faint sweet scent that some people notice. Oily and congestion-prone skin should watch how the slightly heavier texture behaves under sunscreen before committing to it daily.

products.name: DIVE-IN Low Molecular Hyaluronic Acid Toner
products.whatItIs: Torriden's hydration line runs on low molecular weight hyaluronic acid, and the toner is its lightest expression: watery, fast-absorbing, vegan and fragrance-free. The brand's argument is that smaller hyaluronic fragments sit better in the upper layers of skin than large ones. That is a defensible formulation choice rather than a settled advantage, and the toner is pleasant either way.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and combination skin that wants water without weight, and sensitive skin looking for a short, unscented list. It works well in humid climates and disappears under sunscreen. Dry skin will need a richer follow-up. If you already own a good hyaluronic serum, the toner is convenience rather than necessity.
products.howToUse: First step after cleansing, twice daily, patted onto damp skin. Layer two or three times for the 7-skin approach — the texture is thin enough to take it. Seal with a cream afterwards. Compatible with every common active, including retinol, acids and vitamin C.
products.watchOut: 'Low molecular' is a formulation claim that gets sold as penetration science; how far any hyaluronic acid travels from a leave-on toner is not well established. More practically, hyaluronic acid is a humectant — unsealed in dry air it can leave skin feeling tighter than before. Always follow it with something occlusive.

products.name: Advanced Snail 96 Mucin Power Essence
products.whatItIs: The product that made snail mucin a mainstream idea outside Korea. It is almost entirely snail secretion filtrate with a short supporting cast, and the texture is the point: viscous, faintly stringy, and it sinks in far faster than it looks like it will. No acids, no added fragrance, nothing competing with the one ingredient it is named after.
products.whoItSuits: Dehydrated, dull or post-blemish skin that wants a plumping layer without a heavy cream. It suits most skin types, oily included. Two groups should be careful: anyone with an animal-protein sensitivity, and anyone who finds slippery occlusive textures congesting. It is not vegan, which rules it out for some buyers on principle rather than performance.
products.howToUse: After toner, before serums and moisturiser, AM and PM. A few drops pressed in — it spreads much further than it appears to. Let it set for half a minute before the next layer. It plays well with everything and makes a useful buffer on nights you use retinol.
products.watchOut: The 'repair' language around snail mucin outruns the evidence considerably; most published work is small or industry-linked, and the reliable effect is hydration. A minority of users report small bumps or congestion after a few weeks of daily use. COSRX has tweaked the formula over the years, so texture varies slightly between versions.

products.name: Time Revolution The First Treatment Essence
products.korean: 타임 레볼루션 더 퍼스트 트리트먼트 에센스
products.whatItIs: Missha's fermented first essence, and for years the default answer whenever someone asked for a cheaper route into the ferment-essence category. It is watery, quick to absorb, and built on fermented yeast filtrate with bifida ferment alongside. Missha has revised it several times, so the version on the box matters more here than it does for most products.
products.whoItSuits: Normal to dry skin that wants a light glow-and-smoothness layer early in the routine. Mature skin often gets on with it well. It is a poor fit if you are sensitive to fragrance or dislike ferment smells. Oily skin can use it, though it may prefer to skip straight to a lighter serum. Nobody should expect retinoid-grade change.
products.howToUse: After toner, before serums, AM and PM. Decant into the palm and press in — several thin passes work better than one heavy pour. Give it a minute before the next layer. It sits comfortably under vitamin C in the morning and retinol at night.
products.watchOut: The dupe framing is the real problem. This is a different ferment in a different formula, not a copy, and comparisons treating the two as interchangeable are unhelpful. It is fragranced. Ferment essences also attract a lot of vague 'skin renewal' claiming — what is demonstrable is hydration and immediate smoothness, not structural change.

products.name: Time Revolution Artemisia Treatment Essence
products.whatItIs: A calming counterpart to Missha's original first essence, built on artemisia — 쑥 (ssuk), Korean mugwort — instead of ferment. It is watery, herbal-smelling and aimed squarely at skin that is irritated rather than dull. Mugwort has a long history in Korean folk care, which the marketing leans on hard; the formulation itself is a straightforward soothing hydrator.
products.whoItSuits: Reactive, flushed or breakout-prone skin, and anyone whose barrier is having a bad month. Oily skin does particularly well because it is so light. Dry skin will want more on top. The herbal smell is divisive — if you dislike the scent of mugwort you will not tolerate this, because it is unmistakably present in the bottle.
products.howToUse: After toner, before serum, AM and PM. Press in two thin layers rather than one thick one. It makes a sensible buffer on exfoliant nights: essence, wait, active, then moisturiser. Nothing in it conflicts with retinol, acids or vitamin C used at another time of day.
products.watchOut: Mugwort belongs to the Asteraceae family, alongside ragweed and chamomile — if you have a known ragweed or daisy allergy, patch-test carefully before committing. The traditional-medicine framing does not translate into strong clinical evidence for topical use. What you can reasonably expect is comfort and hydration, not resolution of anything.

products.name: First Care Activating Serum
products.whatItIs: Sulwhasoo's flagship first essence, known in Korea as 윤조에센스 (yunjo essence), and the product that established the whole apply-before-everything-else category. It is a herbal blend in a light, faintly oily fluid rather than a ferment, with the brand's hanbang framing — Korean traditional-medicine botanicals, ginseng foremost — carried throughout. It looks watery in the palm and finishes slightly cushioned, which is unlike almost anything else sold as a first step.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, dull or mature skin with the budget for a luxury first step, and anyone who enjoys hanbang textures and scent. It layers well under rich creams. Oily and acne-prone skin generally find it unnecessary. If you are assembling a first routine, this is not where the money should go — sunscreen and a decent moisturiser matter far more.
products.howToUse: The first thing onto cleansed skin, before toner, AM and PM. Two or three drops warmed between the palms and pressed on. Follow with your usual routine. Sulwhasoo's own ritual involves rolling the applicator over the face; whether that adds anything beyond pleasantness is doubtful.
products.watchOut: It is strongly fragranced with a herbal-woody scent that reactive skin may not tolerate. Evidence for the botanical blend is largely traditional and brand-generated rather than independent. A substantial part of the price buys heritage, packaging and feel — all real pleasures, but none of them the same thing as demonstrated performance.

products.name: Bichup Self-Generating Anti-Aging Essence
products.whatItIs: The signature step of The History of Whoo's royal-court hanbang range: a rich, oil-textured essence of herbal extracts applied before the rest of the routine. Presentation is a large part of the product — weighty gold-toned packaging, a ceremonial applicator, a strong traditional-medicine narrative. Underneath it behaves as an emollient herbal essence that leaves a distinctly nourished, slightly filmy finish.
products.whoItSuits: Dry and mature skin that likes rich textures and is buying the ritual as much as the formula. It works well in cold weather and under heavy creams. Oily, combination or breakout-prone skin will almost certainly find it too much. Anyone shopping on evidence rather than experience should look at a peptide or retinoid serum instead.
products.howToUse: Before toner on cleansed skin, AM and PM, two or three drops pressed in. Warm it between the palms first — it spreads better that way. Follow with the rest of your routine. In summer, or in a humid climate, PM only is plenty for most people.
products.watchOut: 'Self-generating' and 'anti-ageing' are marketing constructions rather than descriptions of a demonstrated mechanism; read the claims as cosmetic. It is heavily fragranced. The oily finish congests some people, particularly along the jaw. And the price reflects a luxury gifting market in Korea far more than anything on the ingredient list.

products.name: Bean Essence
products.whatItIs: A single-ingredient-led essence: fermented soybean extract makes up nearly all of it, with almost nothing else on the list. Mixsoon's whole proposition is minimalism and this is its clearest expression. The texture is thick and slightly sticky at first, then settles. It is sold as a softening and smoothing step rather than a hydrating one, though hydration is most of what it actually does.
products.whoItSuits: People who want the shortest possible ingredient list, and skin that reads as rough or tired rather than irritated. Dry and normal skin get on with it best. Anyone with a soy allergy should avoid it outright. If you dislike tacky textures this is not your essence — the first thirty seconds are noticeably sticky.
products.howToUse: After cleansing or toner, AM and PM. A small amount patted over the face and left to settle before the next step. Some people prefer it as a ten-minute leave-on mask a couple of times a week. Follow with moisturiser; on its own it seals nothing in.
products.watchOut: The 'gentle exfoliation' claim attached to fermented bean essences is soft — enzymatic activity in a leave-on product at this concentration is not comparable to an acid, and you should not expect resurfacing. It has a distinct fermented-bean smell that some find unpleasant. Fermented soy is also a plausible irritant for a small number of people.

products.name: Mugwort Essence
products.whatItIs: An essence made almost entirely of mugwort extract, with the sourcing region printed on the box in keeping with I'm From's single-origin approach. It is thicker and darker than most essences, smells strongly of the plant, and is positioned for skin that is angry rather than dry. No acids and no added fragrance — the scent is the mugwort itself, undisguised.
products.whoItSuits: Congested, flushed or reactive skin that wants a calming layer with some substance to it. Oily skin tends to like how it finishes. It is a poor choice for anyone sensitive to strong natural scents, and dry skin will still need a proper moisturiser over it. Do not expect it to clear active acne.
products.howToUse: After toner, AM and PM, a thin layer pressed in. It can also be used as a ten to fifteen minute wash-off mask during a bad skin week, which is how many people get the most out of a bottle. Follow with cream. Compatible with actives, given a moment to absorb.
products.watchOut: The smell is genuinely strong and lingers — a real problem for some people and a perfectly reasonable reason to skip it. Mugwort sits in the Asteraceae family, so ragweed and daisy allergies warrant a patch test. A high percentage of a plant extract is a sourcing story rather than a potency claim, and the price here reflects the story.

products.name: Ginseng Essence Water
products.whatItIs: A watery essence built on ginseng root water with niacinamide, sitting somewhere between a toner and a light essence in both texture and role. Beauty of Joseon's hanbang positioning is more restrained than the luxury houses' — the list is short, the price is low and there is no ritual attached. It absorbs quickly and leaves a soft, slightly dewy finish.
products.whoItSuits: Dry to normal skin wanting an inexpensive hydration-plus-glow step, and anyone curious about hanbang ingredients without a three-figure outlay. Mature skin does well with it. Oily skin can use it in place of a toner. Sensitive skin should note the natural ginseng scent, which is mild but definitely present.
products.howToUse: After cleansing, in place of or straight after your toner, AM and PM. Press two thin layers into damp skin. It works particularly well under the brand's own sunscreen, which is what most people own it alongside. Nothing in it conflicts with vitamin C, acids or retinol.
products.watchOut: Ginseng's topical reputation rests largely on traditional use and a modest research base; expect hydration and a temporary glow rather than firming. The niacinamide is there, but this is not a brightening product in any serious sense. As with the whole brand, formulas get revised — read the current list rather than an old review.

products.name: Red Rice Moisture Firming Essence
products.whatItIs: Hanyul is Amorepacific's hanbang line, and this essence is its rice product: a milky, slightly rich fluid built on red rice extract, aimed at skin that feels slack and dry rather than irritated. It is more substantial than a typical essence and behaves almost like a thin emulsion, which suits the older audience it is clearly written for.
products.whoItSuits: Dry and mature skin wanting comfort plus a softening effect, particularly in cold weather. Normal skin can use it year-round. Oily and combination skin will likely find it heavy as a mid-routine layer. 'Firming' in a cosmetic context means the look of firmness — anyone expecting structural change should read the word that way.
products.howToUse: After toner, before cream, AM and PM. A pump or two pressed in and given a moment to settle. In winter it can double as a light moisturiser for normal skin. Layer a richer cream over it at night if your skin is genuinely dry rather than just dehydrated.
products.watchOut: Rice extracts are a heritage ingredient with a pleasant softening effect and a thin evidence base for anything beyond that. The firming language is cosmetic, not structural. It is fragranced in the hanbang style, which not everyone tolerates. Distribution outside Korea is patchier than the bigger Amorepacific brands, so overseas pricing can be inflated.

products.name: Fundamental Ampule Mist
products.whatItIs: A mist with more in it than water — Klairs positions it as an ampoule you can spray, and the output is a fine, slightly milky mist rather than a bare water spritz. That distinction is the whole argument: plain water mists evaporate and can leave skin drier than before, whereas a mist carrying humectants leaves something behind. Unfragranced, in keeping with the line.
products.whoItSuits: Dry and sensitive skin, air-conditioned offices, long flights, and anyone who tops up hydration through the day. It also works as a light toner step for normal skin. Oily skin rarely needs it. If you want something to set makeup, this is the wrong texture — it is too substantial for that job.
products.howToUse: Whenever skin feels tight: hold it at arm's length, mist, then press in with your palms rather than letting it air-dry. It can serve as a first hydration step after cleansing, or go over makeup if you are careful. Follow with moisturiser at least once during the day.
products.watchOut: Mists are the most over-sold format in skincare. Even a well-made one is a top-up rather than a hydration strategy, and misting repeatedly without sealing can leave skin feeling worse in dry air. The nozzle clogs if the bottle is stored on its side. Cost per millilitre is high for what is largely a convenience product.

products.name: White Truffle First Spray Serum
products.whatItIs: A two-phase spray that shakes into an emulsion of white truffle extract and plant oils, applied as the first step after cleansing. It is the product that made d'Alba a duty-free fixture, and the format is genuinely unusual — an oil-containing serum delivered as a mist, leaving a soft, faintly luminous finish rather than a wet one you have to wait out.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, dull or mature skin that wants a fast one-step glow layer, and travellers who want a serum that survives a carry-on liquids bag. Oily and acne-prone skin should be cautious — the oil phase does not suit everyone. It is a comfort and finish product rather than a treatment for any particular concern.
products.howToUse: Shake hard until the phases combine, mist onto cleansed skin from a short distance, then press in. Two or three sprays, AM and PM, before the rest of your steps. It can also be misted over makeup for a dewier finish, though it will move foundation if you overdo it.
products.watchOut: White truffle is an expensive-sounding ingredient with essentially no independent evidence behind it in skincare — the premium buys a story. It is fragranced. The spray format also means a fair amount of product ends up in the air rather than on your face, which makes the real cost per use higher than the bottle size suggests.

products.name: Green Tea Mineral Mist
products.whatItIs: One of Innisfree's longest-running products: a light mist of Jeju green tea water and mineral water with a small amount of humectant, sold as a daytime refresher rather than a routine step. It is cheap, stocked in every Korean shop and airport, and refreshingly unpretentious about what it is — a fine spray that makes hot skin feel better for a while.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and combination skin in summer, and anyone who wants something to carry rather than something to build a routine around. It is fine over makeup. Dry skin gets very little from it and would do better with a humectant-heavy mist. Sensitive skin should check the current formula for fragrance before buying a bottle.
products.howToUse: Spray from around twenty centimetres whenever skin feels hot or tight, then press in what is left rather than letting it evaporate. Over makeup, mist lightly and blot. It is not a substitute for a toner, and it should never replace a moisturiser at any point in the day.
products.watchOut: This is the format's central problem in its purest form: a mostly-water mist that evaporates takes some of your skin's own moisture with it unless you press it in and seal it. Innisfree has reformulated the line more than once, so the current bottle may differ from older reviews. Enjoyable, and easily the least essential product here.

products.name: N.M.F Aquaring Ampoule Mask
products.whatItIs: Mediheal's best-known hydration mask and one of the highest-selling sheet masks in Korea. The essence is humectant-led — hyaluronic acid, panthenol and the natural-moisturising-factor components the name refers to — on a thin cellulose sheet that clings reasonably well. Nothing in it is exotic; the appeal is a generous volume of well-judged hydrating essence for very little money.
products.whoItSuits: Any skin type that is dehydrated, and particularly useful the night before an event or after a flight. Sensitive skin usually tolerates it, though a patch test is still sensible. Oily skin can use it with little risk of congestion. It is a top-up rather than a solution — no weekly mask changes baseline skin.
products.howToUse: After cleansing and toner, on a clean face, for fifteen to twenty minutes. Take it off before it dries out, press the remaining essence in, then follow with moisturiser to seal it. One to three times a week is plenty. Use the leftover essence in the sachet on your neck.
products.watchOut: Leaving a sheet mask on until it goes crisp reverses the point — the drying sheet begins pulling moisture back out. They are also single-use waste, which mounts up quickly at three a week. Mediheal's range is enormous and the packaging is revised often, so check you have picked up the variant you actually meant to buy.

products.name: Tea Tree Care Solution Essential Mask
products.whatItIs: The blemish-focused sheet in Mediheal's core range: a soothing essence carrying tea tree leaf extract on the same thin cellulose sheet as the rest of the line. It is aimed at skin that is oily and irritated rather than dry, and the essence runs noticeably lighter than the hydrating versions. Tea tree appears here as an extract, not as the essential oil.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and breakout-prone skin wanting a calming twenty minutes, especially during a bad patch. It suits combination skin in summer. Dry skin will find it thin. It is genuinely not an acne treatment, and using it in place of an evidence-based active — a BHA, or something prescribed — is a poor trade.
products.howToUse: On cleansed skin after toner, fifteen to twenty minutes, once or twice a week. Press in the remaining essence and follow with a light moisturiser. Avoid stacking it on the same night as a strong exfoliant; congested skin already being exfoliated does not need more stimulus on top.
products.watchOut: Tea tree has some evidence at meaningful concentrations, mostly as the oil in leave-on products, and a sheet mask essence sits well below that. Expect calm, not clearing. Tea tree is also a known contact allergen for a minority, so patch-test. Persistent acne belongs with a clinician rather than with a box of masks.

products.name: Gummy Sheet Mask Heartleaf Sticker
products.whatItIs: Abib's sheet masks use a thicker, more elastic fabric than the usual thin cellulose, which is where the 'gummy' and 'sticker' naming comes from — it grips the face properly instead of sliding off halfway through. The heartleaf version carries a calming, watery essence. The sheet quality is the genuine differentiator; the essence is a competent, unremarkable soother.
products.whoItSuits: Reactive or flushed skin, and anyone who has given up on masks because they will not stay put — this one holds well enough to move around in. Oily and combination skin do well with it. Very dry skin may prefer a richer variant from the same range. Not a fix for anything, as with all sheet masks.
products.howToUse: Cleansed skin, after toner, fifteen to twenty minutes. The thicker sheet stays wet longer, but do not leave it on until it dries. Press in the residue, then moisturise. Once or twice a week. The range includes rice and madecassoside versions if heartleaf is not the concern you are treating.
products.watchOut: You are paying a premium over cheap cellulose masks for the sheet, not for the formula — worth knowing before buying a box. The essence, like most calming mask essences, works on the appearance of redness for a few hours. Single-use packaging waste is real, and Abib's individual wrappers are heavier than most.

products.name: Dermask Water Jet Vital Hydra Solution
products.whatItIs: Dr.Jart+'s hydration entry in the Dermask range, built around hyaluronic acid at more than one molecular size in a generously soaked sheet. It sits at the derma end of the mask market: sturdier packaging, a better-fitting sheet, and a price several times that of a drugstore equivalent. What is in the essence is sensible rather than novel — humectants doing humectant work.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, tight or travel-worn skin that wants one strong hit of hydration. Normal and combination skin get on with it fine, and sensitive skin usually tolerates it. If you mask several times a week, the cost is hard to justify against a Korean drugstore mask that does most of the same job for a fraction of the money.
products.howToUse: Fifteen to twenty minutes on cleansed skin after toner, then press in the remainder and seal with moisturiser. Best used before an event or after a flight rather than on a fixed schedule. Skip it on nights you are also using a strong active — one new thing at a time.
products.watchOut: The price gap between this and a competent drugstore hydration mask is considerably larger than the formula gap. 'Water Jet' is a product name, not a delivery technology. And hyaluronic acid from a sheet still needs sealing afterwards or the effect is gone by morning — the mask alone is not the whole step.

products.name: Cica Daily Soothing Mask
products.whatItIs: VT's cica mask is sold in large boxes and priced to be used daily, which is unusual — most sheet masks are positioned as an occasional treat. The essence is centella-led with madecassoside, on a thin sheet, and the proposition is frequency rather than intensity — a small dose of the same soothing botanicals, repeated, instead of a strong one now and then. It became a staple partly through the brand's long-running association with BTS.
products.whoItSuits: Skin that is chronically flushed or reactive and responds better to consistent gentle input than to occasional strong input. Oily and breakout-prone skin do well. Dry skin will need a cream over it every single time. If you dislike the ritual of daily masking, a good centella essence delivers the same ingredients with far less packaging.
products.howToUse: After cleansing and toner, ten to twenty minutes, up to once a day if you want. Press in the residue and moisturise afterwards. Nightly use is not required for it to work — three times a week is a reasonable middle ground and makes a box last considerably longer.
products.watchOut: Daily masking is a marketing frame as much as a skincare one; there is no particular reason skin needs a sheet every day, and the cost in wrappers is thirty a month. Centella is well tolerated but a small number of people react to it. Redness that persists deserves a dermatologist's opinion rather than a bigger box.

products.name: Water Sleeping Mask
products.whatItIs: The product that defined the sleeping-mask category outside Korea: a bouncy blue water gel applied as the last PM step, designed to sit on top of the routine and slow overnight water loss. It is a gel rather than an occlusive balm, so it works by holding humectants against skin instead of forming a heavy seal. Laneige has revised it several times.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, combination and mildly dry skin that wants a hydration boost without a rich cream — oily skin often finds it the most comfortable night-time step available. Very dry or mature skin will need an actual occlusive over it or instead of it. Anyone sensitive to fragrance should skip it; the scent is deliberate and prominent.
products.howToUse: The final step at night, over your moisturiser, two or three times a week or nightly if your skin likes it. A thin layer is enough — a thick one mostly transfers to the pillowcase. Cleanse as usual in the morning. It is not a substitute for the moisturiser underneath it.
products.watchOut: The signature fragrance is a formulated feature and a genuine exclusion for reactive skin. Overnight-repair language around sleeping masks generally outruns the evidence — this slows water loss, which is worth having, but skin's own overnight processes happen with or without it. Dry skin usually needs more occlusion than a water gel can provide.

products.name: Ultimate Nourishing Rice Overnight Spa Mask
products.whatItIs: A thick, cream-textured overnight mask built on rice extract with niacinamide, sold as a nourishing final PM step. Where Laneige's is a water gel, this is closer to a rich cream you leave on — heavier, more emollient, better suited to skin that loses moisture overnight. It also works as a short wash-off mask, which is how a good many people prefer to use it.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, dull or winter-worn skin, and mature skin that finds gel masks insubstantial. Normal skin can use it once or twice a week. Oily and congestion-prone skin should be careful — a rich leave-on layer is exactly the sort of thing that clogs some people. Not for anyone already applying a heavy occlusive at night.
products.howToUse: Last step at night over moisturiser, a thin layer, two or three times a week. Alternatively use it as a fifteen-minute wash-off mask and follow with your usual cream. Rinse in the morning. Hold off on stacking it over retinol nights until you know how your skin handles the occlusion.
products.watchOut: It is rich enough to congest oily skin, and the reports of small bumps generally come from people using it every night rather than occasionally. The brightening implication around rice extract is weak — expect softness and a temporary glow, not tone correction. It carries a faint milky scent that a few people notice and dislike.

products.name: SoonJung 10-Free Moist Emulsion
products.whatItIs: The lotion step in ETUDE's sensitive-skin line, formulated to the same minimum-irritant brief as the toner: panthenol and madecassoside, no added fragrance, no colourant, and the exclusion list the '10-free' name refers to. The texture is a genuine emulsion — thinner than a cream, thicker than an essence — which is a step Western routines tend to skip entirely.
products.whoItSuits: Reactive or barrier-stressed skin, and anyone who finds creams too heavy but a serum not quite enough. It suits oily-but-sensitive skin particularly well and works year-round in humid climates. Very dry skin in winter will want a cream on top. There are no actives in it, which is the point rather than an oversight.
products.howToUse: After your essence or serum, before sunscreen in the morning and before any final occlusive at night. A pea-sized amount covers the face. It makes a useful buffer on retinol or acid nights: emulsion, wait, active, then emulsion again over the top if your skin needs it.
products.watchOut: '10-free' is a marketing label rather than a regulated standard — the specific exclusions vary by brand and tell you less than reading the list yourself. As a formula it is comfortable and unambitious; if your skin is calm and you already use a moisturiser, an emulsion adds a step without adding much. Dry skin will still need more.

products.name: Ceramide Ato Lotion
products.whatItIs: Illiyoon is Amorepacific's supermarket-priced ceramide range, and the lotion is its lightest leave-on: a fluid, fast-absorbing ceramide emulsion sold in large bottles for face and body alike. 'Ato' points at atopic-prone skin, which is the audience it is written for. The standard version is unfragranced and priced closer to a body lotion than a facial one, which is exactly why people buy it by the litre.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, flaky or easily irritated skin that goes through moisturiser quickly, and households wanting one bottle for several people. It works on the face for normal to dry skin. Oily skin may find it unnecessary. If you have diagnosed eczema or atopic dermatitis, this is a supportive daily moisturiser and not a treatment — that is a conversation for your doctor.
products.howToUse: After your hydration steps, morning and night, on face or body. Apply to skin still slightly damp after washing, which is when a ceramide emulsion does its best work. Reapply on arms and legs as often as needed. In winter, layer a cream over it on the driest patches.
products.watchOut: The 'Ato' naming reads as a medical claim to some buyers and is not one — it describes the intended audience, not a demonstrated effect, and no cosmetic lotion treats atopic dermatitis. The range has several versions with different textures and scents, so check which bottle you are picking up. For face-only use, the large size may turn before you finish it.
